title: The Boswell trio and joining Eckert's Jazz Band
summary: After his mother smashed his drums he sits in with a band on a truck, quits his bellhop job, buys drums and plays Woodman's Hall for a year.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons

blocks.x: Well, they didn't live across the river then. No. Well, I thought maybe they were from over there. They never did live across, no, the Hardys lived across the river, you see.

I mean, they Hardys probably all did. And, and, and, and Emmett's sister and the Boswell kids were, were, were real friendly. And that's how, how, how Emmett happened to go to the Boswell's house, through his sister. And they had a, they had a, a little trio. They played, they played both. When they played classical, Connie would play the cello, Martha would play the piano, and Vett would play the violin. And when they played jazz, Vett would play the banjo, Connie, uh, Martha would play the piano. And, uh, and, uh, Connie would play the saxophone. Yes and that, and she still got the reed on the saxophone that, was bought. They never had, she never had, she never had, that's, that's the truth. She never has changed the reed. She still got the reed that came with the horn. And, uh, we used to go out there and play. And then, I don't know, Mama, I got, I got, I come home about half loaded one night, Mama got mad. Mama took a axe and bust up the, the drums. So, I, I didn't play for about three or four years. And I was hopping bells at the, at the, at the ground wall. And I walked to the corner and there's a band on the truck. And they don't have any, they don't have any drumming. The drummer didn't show up. And here's who's in the band. Tony Fugierat's the, the cornet player. A fella by the name of Bill Eckert is the leader. They call it Eckert's Jazz Olus. Uh, Marlowe the trombone player. Alfonson. You know him? Leon. He's the trombone player. Lester Bouchon is the clarinet and saxophone player. And Napa Lamar is the, the banjo player. So, they stopped the other day. They were advertising, say, a dance or a fight or something. And, uh, they stopped there to play a tune and they don't have them. So, I asked them, I said, I never had seen any of them before in my life. I said, what's the matter? The drummer didn't show up. I got my, my bellhops uniform out. I was out for lunch, you see. And, uh, he said, no. So, I jumped up there and I sit in and I, I played a couple of tunes with him, you see. So, that was it. I come right back to the hotel. I quit my job. I went up and, uh, Lester was, uh, repairing instruments up at Kahn. The C.G. Kahn Company had, had opened the store here on Barone Street, see. And I went up there and bought a, bought a set of drums and went, uh, went playing with that. And we, there, we, we got a job of four nights a week down there. You ever been on this Woodman's Hall down there at Urquhart and, uh, what's going on? Well, we got a job down there four nights a week. And we played there over, about a year. Maybe a little better than a year. So, they used to, we used to take two intermissions a night where you'd get off the stand, you see. So, they used to give us a, a soft drink. And four dollars a night was, uh, was the price, you see. And, uh, they'd give you a soft drink each intermission. So, they're gonna, they made up their mind, they're gonna cut us down. They're only gonna give us one drink a night instead of the two bottles of root beer or whatever it was, you know. So, we, we, we quit. So, then, Nappy Lamar books a job in a nightclub down on Dolphine Street. I think they call it the cave. Down, down, down in the quarter down there. What's the cave now? I think they, yeah. The tunnel ball isn't there? No, I think it was where the cave is now. I'm pretty sure.
